summary: Describes an architecture for extending pseudowire emulation across multiple packet switched network segments, including cases where each segment belongs to a different provider. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5659 describes how a point-to-point pseudowire can pass through several network segments and providers. Intermediate switching edges join the segments, while the two end devices see one emulated service.

questions: what is the difference between t-pe and s-pe
why use ms-pw instead of ss-pw
subtitle: How a pseudowire can cross several packet-network segments as one service.

tldr.problem: A full mesh of single-segment pseudowires needs many tunnels and signaling adjacencies as provider-edge devices increase.
tldr.mechanism: A multi-segment pseudowire joins segments at switching provider edges, which replace the pseudowire label for the next segment.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes an Informational architecture. It does not specify wire encapsulations or detailed setup mechanisms.

facts.label: Full-mesh growth
facts.value: In proportion to the square of the number of PEs

facts.label: Service state
facts.value: Every segment and PSN tunnel must be operational

today: RFC 5659 is an Informational document published in October 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; it describes architecture and leaves wire formats and detailed setup mechanisms out of scope.

sections.title: Why Use Multiple Pseudowire Segments
sections.content:
A single-segment pseudowire connects two provider-edge devices over one packet-switched network tunnel. If every edge needs a direct pseudowire to every other edge, the number of devices, tunnels, and signaling adjacencies grows in proportion to the square of the number of provider edges.

A multi-segment pseudowire lets intermediate provider edges switch between segments. This supports sparse tunnel meshes, multiple routing domains within one provider, and connections across providers or different packet-network types.
sections.plainLanguage: A direct tunnel between every pair of edge devices creates many connections. Joining shorter segments at intermediate devices can reduce the number of tunnels and signaling relationships.

sections.title: T-PEs, S-PEs, and Segments
sections.content:
A terminating provider edge (T-PE) connects the customer-facing attachment circuit to the pseudowire. A switching provider edge (S-PE) switches the control and data planes between adjacent pseudowire segments and terminates their packet-network tunnels. A segment crosses one tunnel in each direction.

An MS-PW is a static or dynamic set of two or more contiguous segments that behaves as one point-to-point pseudowire. From the Layer 2 VPN perspective, it is indistinguishable from a single-segment pseudowire. Both directions use the same set of S-PEs, although the underlying packet-network tunnel routes need not be reciprocal.
sections.plainLanguage: The T-PEs are the endpoints that connect to the customer service. S-PEs switch traffic between segments, and the complete set of segments acts as one pseudowire between the endpoints.

sections.title: What Happens at a Switching Edge
sections.content:
At an S-PE, a forwarder uses the incoming pseudowire label to select the outgoing segment. The mapping can be configured or dynamic. The S-PE does not process the native service carried inside the pseudowire.

If both packet networks use the same type, the S-PE can swap the label. If they use different types, it removes the incoming demultiplexer, maps it, and adds the outgoing one. Policies such as admission control, rate control, quality-of-service mapping, and security may also be applied there.
sections.plainLanguage: An S-PE uses the incoming label to choose the next segment and changes the label for that segment. It forwards the carried service without processing its native content.

sections.title: Setup, Failure Reporting, and Maintenance
sections.content:
Switching points may be configured in advance or selected dynamically. Labels can be configured or signaled for each segment. The complete service is up only when all segments and their packet-network tunnels work along the path; a bidirectional service also needs both directions working.

If a segment reports a failure, an S-PE must propagate that notification to the next segment when such a mechanism exists. Maintenance tools should test individual segments and the full path, and should identify which S-PEs the pseudowire crosses.
sections.plainLanguage: The entire service depends on every segment and tunnel along its route. Operators need to check both individual segments and the end-to-end connection.

sections.title: Congestion and Trust Across Providers
sections.content:
Congestion in a packet network can affect its control plane. Each segment needs congestion detection and control when capacity cannot be provisioned in advance. S-PEs should pass congestion information along the path; an S-PE at the edge of a congested network may respond more quickly.

The architecture assumes trust among the initiator, T-PEs, and S-PEs. A switching edge should select only a next hop that the originator considers eligible. At provider boundaries, the RFC calls for peer authentication and mechanisms to ensure that a pseudowire is switched to the correct outgoing segment.
sections.plainLanguage: Congestion in one segment can affect the whole service, so devices need to detect it and pass that information onward. Providers also need to authenticate neighboring switching devices and enforce their policies.
